reviews.title: Better Alternative Than A MacBook Pro
reviews.content:
I recently purchased the 2025 ASUS ROG Zephyrus G14 with the RTX 5080 while it was on sale at Best Buy for about $2,650, versus a $3,170 MSRP.

This is my first Windows laptop. I bought it primarily as a compact mobile workstation rather than a gaming PC, although I’ll game on it occasionally. I specifically chose the 5080 for its 16GB of VRAM and additional CUDA capability. Unfortunately, it doesn’t appear ASUS will offer the same discrete 5080 in a 14-inch chassis for 2026. I hope they reconsider.

My first impression is that the $2,650 sale price is much closer to what this machine should cost. It’s excellent, but at $3,170 I would seriously consider a true mobile workstation instead.

Build quality is very good. The aluminum chassis is compact, lightweight and feels comparable to my wife’s MacBook Pro. Nothing feels cheap or like ASUS cut corners. The bottom panel is also held on with accessible screws, which should make cleaning and maintenance easier. The keyboard is responsive with a shallow, crisp feel. I’m not a fan of the light bar on the lid—it feels a little tacky to me—but that’s subjective and it can be turned off.

Performance is excellent for the size. It won’t replace my custom desktop in outright performance, but it does exactly what I expected from a 14-inch workstation-class laptop. I also haven’t experienced the stuttering, display problems or other strange behavior some owners have reported.

Armoury Crate has worked perfectly for me. In Silent mode, the G14 sips power. I’ve seen roughly 6–8 hours of light use running cloud applications such as Codex and Claude, YouTube, several Edge windows and email. The fans are often inaudible or completely off.

One important Windows 11 note: from the factory, closing the lid uses Modern Standby/Sleep, which can allow the laptop to remain active and warm. I changed the lid-close behavior to Hibernate before putting it in a bag. This is a Windows behavior, not specifically a G14 defect.

In Performance mode while unplugged, I’ve seen around 4–6 hours, probably closer to four under heavier use. The GPU understandably does not boost as aggressively on battery.

Turbo mode requires AC power and really wakes the machine up. Under sustained compute workloads I measured the RTX 5080 at essentially 99–100% utilization with power around its 120W limit. I occasionally saw brief telemetry spikes above 120W, although Armoury Crate reports a 120W maximum. More importantly, the GPU maintained its performance under sustained loads.

Thermals impressed me. With the laptop on a flat surface, the RTX 5080 generally remained in the mid-70°C range during long 99–100% GPU workloads and showed no meaningful thermal throttling. That’s impressive for this much GPU in such a small chassis. CPU-heavy workloads produced more heat, with the Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 occasionally reaching around 80°C, still well within normal operating range. Under light use I typically see the CPU around the upper 40s.

Fan behavior is also better than I expected. Silent mode is genuinely quiet. Performance and Turbo naturally get louder as workload increases, and at full load the fans are definitely loud, but the sound quality is smooth and consistent. I haven’t heard bearing noise, chatter or annoying pitch changes. They sound like a premium cooling system doing its job.

The touchpad on my unit is large, responsive and solid with none of the looseness some users have reported. The speakers are loud and crisp. The OLED display is excellent, very bright, smooth, and HDR looks fantastic.

Overall, ASUS did an impressive job fitting this level of hardware into a 14-inch machine. The compact size, 16GB RTX 5080 and strong cooling system are the biggest reasons I chose it.

At the sale price: 5/5.
At the full $3,170 MSRP: 4/5.

At the discounted price, I would absolutely recommend the G14 over the competing options I considered.

reviews.title: Best for Local LLMs + Gaming + Productivity
reviews.content:
I bought the ASUS ROG Z13 Flow with 128gb Unified RAM mainly for one purpose — "to run LLMs locally" — and honestly, it has exceeded my expectations.

I’ve downloaded and tried multiple models, and currently allocated 64 GB as VRAM to load "Gemma 4 26B Q4". I was honestly surprised by the speed. I’m getting around "42 – 45 tokens/sec", which I did not expect from a device this size. Really impressed with the performance.

My kids also loving it for gaming while I'm away from desk. On our previous laptop with 8 GB VRAM, we were getting 60 - 100 FPS in most of the games. With the Z13, we’re seeing 380+ FPS in the games we play. That’s a huge upgrade and the gaming performance is really impressive.

One thing that surprised me the most is how quiet the system is, even while gaming heavily. I was expecting a lot more fan noise and heat, but in my experience it has been surprisingly quiet and doesn’t get uncomfortably hot. This is especially nice when using it during a driving trip.

I also really like the detachable keyboard. With the USB ports and HDMI, it feels like much more than just a tablet. I can use it as a proper productivity machine when needed and then easily switch back to tablet mode.

Though its not OLED, with 500nit, 180hz refresh makes display a breeze... ultimate beauty with brain!

Overall, I’m really loving the Z13. The combination of local AI performance, gaming, portability, and the 2-in-1 design makes it a very impressive machine for what I wanted to use it for.

So far, I’m very happy with the purchase. Strongly recommend.

reviews.title: Very fast and responsive, but know its limits
reviews.content:
It is a very good, fast, and responsive machine. However, if you are looking at the 128GB version specifically for heavy AI workloads or high-end gaming, there are a few things you should know.
​I originally wanted to run large local LLMs. While the laptop is fully capable of running them, pushing anything above 30 to 38 billion parameters just isn't reasonable. The models will load, but the generation speed is far too slow to be practical. Because of this bottleneck, the 128GB version wasn't as useful to me as I hoped. If you want to run LLMs, a laptop with an RTX 5090 is a much better buy; it can run those same 30B+ models, but it will process them significantly faster.
​As for gaming, it is generally great, but it does have some frustrating restrictions. I ran into issues where certain AAA games were unplayable at medium settings. If your main focus is gaming, you will get a much better and more reliable experience out of a standard laptop equipped with an RTX 5070.
​Ultimately, it’s a cool and capable device, but you might be better off saving your money on the RAM upgrade and buying a dedicated gaming or AI laptop depending on your specific needs.

q_a.question: can you connect a larger monitor to it
q_a.answer:
PHYSICAL size of either the computer OR the monitor have absolutely no correlation to connectivity, or performance. 

You could connect a 5" portable monitor/tv that is less than FHD in resolution, or one that is hundreds of feet large with 8K clarity. The important factors are the specs on both, and the connections between them. At the same time, you could use a Kindle Fire, or the best gaming computer around, as the source. Of course, with a giant monitor, you would be stretching the limits of the Fire's resolution, so there would be blurriness in the image, as well as vertical black bars on either side to maintain the aspect ratio of the original source. Furthermore, while the native monitor on this OmniBook (and most non-premium laptops) is limited to FHD@60Hz to save on cost and battery life, the GPU is capable of considerably more, even if integrated with the CPU, easily at 4K with 60Hz or even 8K. Keeping the laptop also helps in overcoming the native limitations for more demanding output.

Then there is the connection to consider. HDMI 1.4 is limited to 4K at 30Hz or 1080p at 60Hz. HDMI 2.0 / 2.1 (which is what is on this specific model) or USB-C (DisplayPort): easily allows output of 4K at 60Hz, 120Hz, or higher without breaking a sweat.

q_a.question: Who makes the NVME, does it have DRAM, if there is DRAM how much of it?
q_a.answer:
You will never get a definitive answer to this question. You might as well ask whether it has a Samsung drive,  or Kingston memory.
Computer manufacturing is a multimillion dollar business (at LEAST). This means companies can't just sit on inventory while they wait for a specific part from Crucial, Western 
Digital, etc.; instead, they buy whatever part meets their spec and is available when they need it. So one person who has this model (and knows where and how to look for it) might answer the question and say "yes, it has DRAM and it is has 16MB," while another will say "no, it doesn't." Both can be absolutely true: one person's drive has it, the other's doesn't.

q_a.question: Is the 16Gb ram in this laptop is 1 x 16 gb installed or 2 x 8gb installed? Please tell me Asap. And also is there an extra slot or SSD inside the laptop or not?
q_a.answer:
The RAM installed is 2×8GB modules of DDR5-5600. The brand of RAM is Samsung, and the RAM model number is M425R1GB4PB0-CWMOL.

There is only 1×M.2 2280 Gen 4 SSD slot running on x4 channels. The installed brand of SSD installed is Sandisk, which is a 512GB module with the model number SDEPNSJ-5126-1006. Some people have mentioned that their machine has a Samsung M.2 card.

If Upgrading:

Be sure to note that the RAM modules supported are 2×8GB DDR5-5600, 2×16GB DDR5-5600, and 2×32GB DDR5-4800. If you upgrade to the max capacity, you will not be able to use the Overclocked RAM speeds, and the motherboard officially supports DDR5-4800 up to 64GB total or DDR5-5600 [Overclocked] up to 32GB total.

Be sure to note that the maximum supported SSD drive capacity is 4TB, and it must be Gen 4 or earlier, this will support a Gen 5 module, but it will perform at Gen 4 speeds. Do not use a SSD with a heatsink, as it will not fit properly, and will not be cooled properly.

I hope you find this information useful. I do not work for Best Buy and am not associated with them at all. It took trial and error along with research to find the information pertaining to the RAM speeds supported by the motherboard.

q_a.answer:
Method 1: Start Menu
Click the Windows (Start) button on the taskbar.
Click the Power icon (⏻).
Select Shut down.
Method 2: Keyboard Shortcut
Press Alt + F4 while on the desktop (minimize or close any open windows first).
In the "Shut Down Windows" dialog, select Shut down.
Click OK or press Enter.
Method 3: Power Button
Press the laptop's power button once briefly.

q_a.question: Are there an geographic restrictions to where this Windows 11 LIcense can be activated and used. I'm interested in buy this laptop as a gift for someone who resides in another country?
q_a.answer: The Windows license built into a computer travels with it and is valid anywhere in the world. It is permanently injected into the motherboard's physical hardware chips by the factory, it is not region-locked, and Microsoft will automatically activate it over the internet whether you boot it up in Europe, Asia, Africa, or the Americas. If purchased in another country, however, you may not be able to change the language if you travel outside that country without an additional cost. Also, if you are concerned about MS365 (formerly Office), that IS Region-Locked. it will often fail to activate if your Microsoft Account's location or IP address points to a different continent. Finally, while Lenovo includes an International Warranty Service (IWS) on many machines, it has severe limitations: Lenovo will only repair your laptop in another country if that exact model variant is also officially sold and supported by Lenovo in that destination country, and because your IdeaPad is a US-market consumer model, a Lenovo repair facility in another country may refuse to service it simply because they do not stock the US-spec replacement motherboards or keyboards.

q_a.question: Can you stop calling Full High Definition as the acronym 2K? It is very misleading, as that is not a standard resolution name and can be mistaken for QHD aka 2560x1440
q_a.answer:
Hey mpetersen71,

We appreciate your inquiry and concern that you've shared. To address this, we'd like to share some reasoning as to why 2K has taken off and is now used widely across the computing space. 

2K resolution is one of multiple high-definition image resolution standards. The primary difference is that 2K resolution can refer to more than one image size. For this reason, 2K is generally accepted as an umbrella term. It is typically used when referring to the motion picture industry, as many films are projected at this standard.

These resolutions are defined by the Digital Cinema Initiatives, or DCI, a governing body comprised of major motion picture studios. The 1920x1200 resolution is considered as 2K, as the horizontal resolution (number of pixels across the display) meets the parameters to fall under the 2K umbrella. 

If you'd like to learn even more, you can visit the following Lenovo web address for details: 
https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/faqs/pc-life-faqs/what-is-2k-resolution/?orgRef=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.google.com%252F | 

We hope that this helps, and if you have any other questions, please feel free to reach out!

reviews.title: Versatile, responsive, and built like a tank
reviews.content:
I needed a machine that could seamlessly transition between a work laptop and a media device, and the Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1 delivers on all fronts.
What stands out:
360° Hinge Flexibility: The hinge is sturdy with no wobble, flipping easily between clamshell, tent mode for watching shows, and flat tablet mode for digital notes or sketches.
Touchscreen & Display: The touch input is ultra-responsive, colors are crisp, and working across multiple documents on the 16:10 aspect ratio feels natural.
Solid Everyday Speed: Multitasking is smooth and effortless. It handles dozens of open tabs, office software, and streaming simultaneously without bogging down.
Battery & Connectivity: It easily clears a standard workday off the charger. Having both Thunderbolt 4 and full-size USB-A / HDMI means no hunting for dongles.
Good to know:
As a 2-in-1 with an all-metal chassis, it has some heft, so it works best on a desk or your lap rather than holding it in one hand like a small tablet.
RAM is soldered on-board, so make sure to configure enough memory from day one to match your long-term needs.
An outstanding balance of build quality, performance, and convertible convenience for the price.

reviews.title: 83ct preferred over amd yoga 7 counterpart
reviews.content:
This particular model bumps to 24gb ram over typical entry point of 16gb, so that's a plus. Like 2 in 1 features too (oled with pen support). 

I also have its amd counterpart (83jr) and there are some things missing there compared to Intel based 83ct that I did not realize before but which are important enough for me to prefer this one.

First, 83jr has a really bad integrated Bluetooth/wifi. Wifi part is fine but Bluetooth is stuttering after waking up from hibernation, which would happen after a few hours of standby . I found no solution to this despite extensive research. Happy to report this Intel box doesn't have this issue.

Second, it has usb4 thunderbolt 4 ports, which works fine with dual 4k docking station that I share with Macbook pro and desktop with tb4 card in it. The 83jr amd chipset only has a dp 2.1 10gbit alt-mode usb 3.2 multi-stream port. In general, dp standards over USB compatibility is a mess, in particular, the multi-stream support. In short you can't have a single docking station that sully supports both thunderbolt and alt mode multi-stream fully. Meaning if you have a tb4 docking for Mac/pcs, this model works fully, but the amd one would require two wires for two displays to work. 
Happily, this 83ct is fully tb4 compatible, so no monitor issues /workarounds.

q_a.question: I recently purchased the Lenovo ideal had Slim 3X with the Snapdragon,X-X126100Qualcom processor. When the specs say there are 2 M.2 slots, does this mean they are expansion slots. If not what does 2 M.2 slots mean. Do all SSD laptops have 2 M.2 slots?
q_a.answer:
Hey Rob,

When the specifications list M.2 slots specifically in terms of storage slots, this refers to the types of storage that system will support and how many drives. In this case, the IdeaPad Slim 3x features two M.2 2242 PCIe 4.0 x4 slots, meaning that if one of slots is preoccupied by the included 256GB drive, there is an open storage slot for storage expansion. Also, many modern systems that have SSDs will feature M.2 storage slots, as this form of storage is more compact, efficient, and performant than traditional SSDs. 

Please feel free to reach out to us with any other questions!

reviews.title: Googlebook Shows Promise, but Not Quite Ready
reviews.content:
It’s 2026, and Google has introduced Googlebooks, a new companion for your Android phone. There aren’t any budget Googlebooks available at the moment, and the Lenovo is no exception. The hardware is nice, featuring an attractive design headlined by a beautiful 3K OLED display running at 120Hz. It has an oversized haptic trackpad, 16GB of memory, and is one of the lightest 15” laptops I’ve ever held. Unfortunately, it’s also expensive, and doesn’t have a higher-end CPU to match its price.

The software is entirely new. It’s Android for the desktop, now called Googlebook OS. The operating system itself is refreshing to use, especially if you enjoy the experience on Google’s latest Pixel devices. In fact, it nearly looks identical, right down to a lot of the same settings. There are even leftover phone artifacts such as options for a mobile hotspot, despite the laptop not having a cellular modem, and options to turn on “Data Saver”.

One of the big selling points of a Googlebook is the deep integration with your Android phone. You can cast apps from your phone to the desktop, interact with your notifications, and manage files or photos on your phone. In practice, however, I found these features didn’t always work particularly well. A lot of times casting wouldn’t work, and I’d be prompted to scan a QR code to re-pair my Pixel phone to the laptop. Notifications were inconsistent, sometimes appearing and sometimes not. Even when they did appear, interacting with them did not always work. Reddit, for example, would send a notification from my phone, but clicking on it would simply cause my phone’s screen to light up as it attempted to cast the application. Then ultimately nothing happened, likely because I didn’t have Reddit installed on the Googlebook. Worse, the notification would then disappear from both devices.

Performance has been just ok. The laptop feels snappy for the most part, but looking at the included CPU and running some benchmarks, it’s not substantially more powerful than my Google Pixel Pro 11. It also has the same amount of memory. Considering that it runs many of the same apps, likely at a similar speed, the primary advantages over my phone are the larger display, included keyboard, and trackpad.

Battery life has been outstanding. This was a surprise to me because the laptop uses an Intel processor, rather than an ARM-based Snapdragon chip. Combined with the lightweight design, this is easily one of the biggest selling points for this laptop. 

Installing apps involves visiting the Play Store, just as you would on an Android phone. There are now labels in the Play Store that indicate whether an app is compatible, “Optimized for Desktop”, or “Made for Desktop”. The latter should provide the best experience, but unfortunately, there are very few of these available. Most first-party apps such as Chrome are “made for desktop”, along with a lot of image editors like Canva. However, many still feel like web apps originally designed with ChromeOS in mind. Even Chrome has issues. For example, video on some websites would play at a very poor framerate (although Youtube works fine, it’s a Google product after all)

A lot of apps are “optimized” but that doesn’t mean they’re fully featured desktop applications. It typically means the interface is responsive and scales appropriately and that it supports the built-in keyboard and trackpad. Microsoft Word, an “optimized” app, is a perfect example. The experience is surprisingly poor, which is particularly disappointing considering writing documents for school or work would be one of the primary reasons to use a Googlebook.

In fact, I wrote this review in Word on the Googlebook. The experience was a bit frustrating. I could not select text normally or copy/paste with the regular keyboard shortcuts. Typing would lag at times, while strange graphical artifacts would be visible from time to time. The application’s functionality itself is stripped down compared to the desktop version on Mac or Windows. Honestly, it’s so bad you just want to pull out a real laptop to get work done.

I was particularly excited about the built-in Linux environment, thinking that I could install anything through the terminal that I couldn’t find in the Play Store. Apps such as VS Code and Gimp would provide me with some familiarity for development and photo editing. Unfortunately, at this time, Linux feels like a second-class citizen, at best used for CLI only commands. While I managed to get both installed, I could not get Code to run and Gimp had a lot UI interface issues. If you do want to code, Google's Antigravity app works if that’s what you’re comfortable using.

The speakers are better than I expected. They could use a bit more bass response but for the most part they work well.

Another area where the Googlebook excels is the Gemini experience. Google’s flagship AI is integrated directly into the operating system, with features like Magic Pointer, which lets you interact with anything on your screen and Rambler, which is smart AI dictation and my favorite feature from this year's Pixel phones. You can also create custom desktop widgets using natural language. If you’re heavily invested in Gemini and Google’s AI features, there’s definitely something to appreciate here.

Pros:
- Extremely lightweight premium design
- Gorgeous 3K OLED 120Hz Display
- App-casting from Android phone
- Good multi-monitor support
- Great sounding speakers
- Built-in Gemini integration
- Instant on functionality
- Excellent battery life
- Large haptic Trackpad
- Linux Support
- Biometric login
- Thunderbolt 4 and Wifi 7
- Includes 1 year of Google AI Pro

Cons:
- Midrange CPU and integrated graphics
- Limited desktop ecosystem for Android
- Early Adopter Bugs – like keyboard lag and inconsistent phone integration
- Linux is mostly limited to CLI terminal emulator
- Expensive

Overall – I find myself enjoying the Googlebook and while simultaneously wondering if I could ever actually use it as my primary device. The hardware is excellent, battery life is fantastic, and Googlebook OS is different and refreshing to use. But it all comes down to the apps. While casual users may find everything they need, the lack of true desktop apps at this early stage of the products lifecycle can make the experience frustrating for all but the most dedicated Android enthusiasts. With more time and especially developer support this could be a true competitor to Mac and Windows based systems.

reviews.title: Nice hardware but missed opportunity
reviews.content:
Title: Nice hardware but missed opportunity

Verdict: The Lenovo Googlebook is a beautiful computer with decent specs and great Google ecosystem integration. However, it lacks the ability to run real programs and the AI features were disappointing. I would recommend this to users heavily invested in the Google ecosystem and that do not have a requirement for heavy programs.

First impressions. I like the white laptop. It’s a nice size, but it’s not heavy. Cool startup logo! 

Setup. You can setup from an iPad or Android device, so probably mobile first approach. During initial setup, you can opt out of signing into a Google account. The computer will provide options to setup fingerprint unlock and/or face unlock, both of which work quite well.
- Setup without an account: If you select this option, a warning box will advise that you will not have access to seamless Google services until you sign in. From there you can add your name and essentially setup a permanent local account. I tried this to see how it worked, and essentially, this computer is mostly a browser if it doesn’t include you Google sign-in (access to sheets, doc, or other Google product requires sign-in).

- Setup with an account: Definitely the way to go. Once you get to your desktop, you can get to all your Google data: email app to your Gmail, files in Google Drive, all your Chrome history, Youtube account, etc. Fundamentally, I think this is the best way to use this computer for one or several users. This way, any user that logs in will immediately have all of their Google account, tools, and data available.

Usage. I love that there is a tutorial video as soon as the laptop loads. However… the video demos are too small! I can barely read what’s in the video, yet half the screen on my computer is white space!! That doesn’t make sense. Coming from an exclusive Windows computer experience, there is definitely a small learning curve… There seems to be no right click, and I keep trying because it’s faster and makes sense to me, for example removing Drop Box from the taskbar… Can’t right click to do that with the touchpad and nearly impossible to figure out how to remove it (had to Google it! And it’s clicking with two fingers at once…). However, when you add a physical mouse (or BT mouse), you can instantly right click and remove it… I don’t understand why not just keep right click on the touchpad to ease the transition from Windows.

Power users. Since we are heavily invested in Google workspace, appsheet tools, scripts, etc., I have been wondering if we could switch to using these at work. It appears that you can still load something like Microsoft Office through the Google store (must have for us to execute advanced formatting). Adobe Acrobat just had the reader; I could not find the pro version. An Adobe Acrobat browser plugin does exist for Chrome but it’s not the same thing. I think we could switch some users because they use mostly web-based apps, but other users need installed programs. 

AI Tools. Access to Gemini pro and Nano Banana for a year is a very nice perk that sweetens the deal. 

Things I love:
- Nice Lenovo hardware
- Beautiful 3K OLED screen
- Good-looking laptop, and it feels really nice
- Super lightweight for its size
- Performs better than its specs
- Security and anti-virus built-in
- Decent specs
- Thank you for the privacy shutter!

Things I don’t like:
- The black bar at the top of the screen takes away from screen real-estate. I understand that they want to give the ecosystem a mobile vibe, but that is so impractical and counter-productive. Put the time, date, and WiFi, and notifications back in the task bar so I can get some real-estate back
- I was interested to try Magic Pointer but it doesn’t work for me… I can’t turn it on.
- I was disappointed with the Built-In Gemini. It’s not really on par with another AI you download and it can use tools such as the web browser  to check things for you.

Overall, this is a nice start for this Googlebook by Lenovo… Nice hardware and very nice integration with the Google ecosystem. However, I think it could be so much more by fully empowering Gemini and AI tool use on the laptop, and more real programs for power users. I would recommend this to users heavily invested in the Google ecosystem and that do not have a requirement for heavy programs.

reviews.title: Gorgeous, But Held Back Slightly by Early Quirks
reviews.content:
I want to completely love this laptop, and most days I think I do. It solves my portability needs beautifully. The sleek Cloud Grey metal chassis has a surprisingly soft-to-the-touch feel, and its lightweight design makes it effortless to carry around, which is a massive win for someone with hand dexterity issues. The 3K OLED screen is gorgeous, and the Gemini AI integration is fantastic and lightning-fast.

However, the occasional software and connection hiccups keep it from absolute perfection. One of the main reasons I purchased this was for seamless continuity with my phone. While it works wonderfully when it cooperates, the connection can be hit-or-miss and laggy at times, forcing me to manually reconnect. Additionally, powered by Intel, it handles day-to-day tasks fine, but it does feel a bit less snappy compared to Snapdragon-powered alternatives I’ve tested.

As for all the not-so-positive reviews the Lenovo is getting, that's not a thing for me. My comments are based on my own empirical observations. I expect some wrinkles, and I believe they are going to be worked out. My suggestion is just to try it and see if it works for you.

Overall, it's a "soft" 4 stars because the hardware fundamentals and portability are just that good. Because I purchased it with a Best Buy Total Membership Protection Plan, I have peace of mind and some time to see if future updates iron out these early wrinkles.

reviews.title: Great Hardware, software is not there yet.
reviews.content:
Here we go again!  I decided to be a beta tester for Google.  I purchased a Googlebook.  I actually purchased the Acer Googlebook first.  I liked the Hardware mostly, but had issues with my phone not connecting.  I did not go into deep troubleshooting because I was turned off by the amount of fingerprints on the blue finish in just a short amount of time.  As I said, very nice hardware minus the fingerprint part, but I returned it. I got the Lenovo version.

For $1099 I considered the price still fair based on the specs.  I did get a Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 prior and for a mere $541 open box.  With the Chromebook the OLED screen is beautiful and very responsive.  It is a great all arounder, and if you can find it for <$700, I highly recommend it.  

Back to the Lenovo Googlebook.  I really loved the magnesium alloy material and how it had a soft touch. The white color was really nice.  For a larger laptop it is amazingly light. For comparison it weighs almost the same amount as the 14 inch Chromebook Plus model.  My only issue with the hardware is that the haptic touchpad on my model had a sort of hollow rattle on one corner, which is odd for a haptic touchpad. 

I was also pleasantly surprised by the display as I normally am more into glossy displays.  This one is anti-glare.and with the high resolution gives the images a soft yet sharp look.   Using the laptop with 120hz does not feel all that special as the Chromebook Plus 14 scrolls the page faster.  The googlebooks are not the only ones that are guilty of this as the Surface Laptop 7 I had was the same when using the touchpad to scroll.  The Surface Pro does not have this issue in either touch or trackpad use.  Weirdly the Chromebook one scrolls significantly faster despite the 60hz. 

I tried so much with this laptop to make it work, but I had the same issue that my phone would not remain paired.  This is the reason I wanted a googlebook.  I like having a laptop that does not have the bloat of windows and I want to use it unlike MacOS.  The question for me isn't who are Googlebooks for, but rather why does it not work consistently with pairing like my car does with AA when I get in.  The brief time it worked right it was nice having my phone's apps visible and all the android apps installed.  It felt like an extension of my phone.  That is all I want.  No complicated OS just browsing and using connected apps. 

Right now I would wait on Googlebooks to get more reliable software to work the way they are advertised to.  The Lenovo Chromebook 14 Plus works more reliably than the Googlebook so there is work to be done here.

reviews.title: On the right track!
reviews.content:
When I heard about the Googlebooks coming out, I got excited. “This is what I’ve been waiting for - for a very long time” I exclaimed! I've tried Chromebooks before and I just don't like Chrome OS. A big blank home screen or desktop just doesn't seem very productive. I love Android. The ability to have the widgets that you want and have folders right on your desktop is what I've been looking for without being a Windows machine. So I definitely wanted to get the Lenovo Googlebook.
So far trying this out, there are some good things and some not so good things. It definitely isn't fully baked yet, but if you like seeing how technology progresses, it's kind of neat to get it now and see how they'll improve it. Think of it like a prototype.
The overall build quality is so-so for me right away. I love that it's nice and light, but the coating that they use on the outside that makes it so nice and smooth, I wish it had a little bit more texture so it's a little more grippy. Being so smooth and whatever the coating is, it actually makes the "premium" magnesium/aluminium blend feel like plastic. If you tap your fingers on the underside of it or on the cover, I swear it's plastic. I like the little tab running across the top. When it's closed, it makes it so easy to open this with one finger. I don't really understand the glow bar on the back of the screen facing away from you. Among other things I thought it was supposed to show the battery charge, but while it's charging up, the glow bar is off. It does not show any kind of level. Hopefully, that is definitely something they add more features to, to make it have a point.
I like the Lenovo Googlebook due to its size. I love the big screen. It gets nice and bright and nice and dim in dark environments. The screen is beautiful. It has an amazing picture, very vibrant and a responsive touchscreen. Also, the face unlock works great as long as you're in a bright room, but in the morning when it's dark and I try to open it, it does not work at all. I always have to put my pin in. The bigger size gives you a well-spaced out keyboard. It's easier to type on. Key travel and clickiness is very nice. Love the fact that it's backlit and easily adjustable. The big trackpad is nice, but I think this could use some work. The haptics on it don't feel premium; it feels a little hollow and kind of cheapy. One and two fingers on it is great, but the three finger gestures I don't care for. It's awkward to try to use those. It should just have the same swipe gestures as the screen can have. It's nice to have a fingerprint reader right on the keyboard, but it is very slow. 
The battery life is pretty good. I use my laptop for my admin every morning for a couple hours and I get just about four days out of it before I have to recharge it. If I were to use it all in one time, I'd probably get about nine to ten hours out of it. When you close the lid and it goes into sleep mode, that's nice, it only loses about 6 to 7% of battery life. Recharging it is pretty quick; I plug it in and it charges up in about an hour and 20 minutes from 15%.
When it comes to actually using the Google Book and the experience, I would say it's mostly positive with a few annoyances that hopefully Google will be fixing with updates. I would have liked to have seen more updates during the about a week I've had it, but I haven't seen anything come through yet. 
Setting up the Googlebook was just like setting up an Android phone, that went super easy. Most apps went over, there's only a few that I had to go and download. But here is the first annoyance, that this is running Android 17 but it doesn't run all Android apps. Some of the main ones like YouTube and Gmail are still progressive web apps or PWAs, and I don't like those. That's what they use on Chrome OS. I want the Android apps. Google absolutely needs to fix this. Continue on seems to work pretty well, although I had to go into my Pixel phone and turn on the feature because it wasn't on right away. But it is really nice to be able to be browsing the web on your phone and think, "Oh, I want to see this bigger," and just go right to the laptop. 
The cast apps feature is bad. It's a great thought but it needs a lot of work. When I try to use it, the apps will come up but there will be missing elements, big blank spaces, or they're just very jittery and unusable. 
The Googlebooks come with Rambler baked in and that is one of my favorite features ever. I use it all the time and it needs to be made available for any electronic device used for communication. It is just so great!
The notifications on the Googlebook need a lot of work as well. I will get double notifications, or I will get notifications that pop up every time I start using it in the morning that I have dismissed hours ago. As long as you're using the Googlebook and your phone together, you can swipe the notifications away, but done separately, the Googlebook has to play catch up.
There is only one volume, (which was I think a thing back in the early 2000s). Come on Google, what happened to the separate volumes for notifications and media and alarms? I hate having the volume up louder when I'm watching something or listening to music and then later a notification will come through blaring loud. I've had to shut them off until they get that fixed.
Casting from the Googlebook to other devices like your TV isn't a great experience. It only finds specifically Google products. If I try to cast something from my Pixel phone, it will show all the Google things and my Fire Sticks and all my devices that I can cast to.

For about a week, I have tried to exclusively use this Lenovo Googlebook and leave my tablet on the table and see if it can replace it, and so far it has been able to. I have some preferences for the tablet, but if Google pushes out updates and fixes these issues, it will absolutely be a wonderful machine.

reviews.title: Hardware top notch except for one thing
reviews.content:
The only show stopper for me is that I could get it to work with my travel external display to work with my USB c connection.

Set up was a breeze. The only hiccup was couldn't get Better Together to work with my Pixel 9 Pro XL but finally worked after rebooting the laptop.

I am using this as my secondary laptop so this is great. Hardware is great but software I know I am one of the early adaptors. I owned a MacBook pro years ago having the same feeling that knowing not everything is going to be compatible.

reviews.title: Fresh Laptop Experience
reviews.content:
I've used plenty of laptops over the years, and the Lenovo Googlebook 15 immediately felt different in a good way. This isn't replacing my main computer, but it has quickly become a device I genuinely enjoy picking up for everyday use.
 The first thing that stood out was how incredibly light it feels for a 15.3-inch laptop. It's easy to carry around the house, use on the couch, or throw into a bag for travel without feeling like i'm hauling around a large-screen notebook. The size-to-weight ratio is really impressive.
 The second thing I noticed was the haptic touchpad. Instead of a traditional physical click, Lenovo uses a haptic system that provides feedback electronically. It feels smooth, modern, and surprisingly premium. After using it for a while, going back to a traditional clickpad feels a bit dated. The touchpad alone gives the laptop a very polished feel.
 The 15.3-inch OLED display is another highlight. Colors are vibrant, blacks are deep, and the 120Hz refresh rate makes scrolling and navigation feel fluid. I was surprised while i was using the Youtube app it was giving me the option to watch content in 8K which by the way it was very impressive!
 Lenovo pairs that gorgeous display with a great set of speakers (dolby atmos) and that's a wining combination, in my opinion adds to the already Premium feeling of this laptop. 
 Bottom Line: 
 -The Lenovo Googlebook 15 feels Fresh, modern, and enjoyable to use. Its lightweight design, beautiful OLED display, and outstanding haptic touchpad make it an excellent choice for anyone wanting a premium everyday laptop experience😁

reviews.title: Excellent Build Quality
reviews.content:
I think Lenovo built the best looking Googlebook and sitting it next to my Lenovo Chromebook Plus, its the exact same design, with a color shade difference. Lately it seems the design of laptops makes it hard to actually use on the lap, as the fans pull from the bottom and right where they would sit on the lap.. Lenovo’s fan placement is technically pulls from the bottom. I’ve seen a lot of reviewers saying that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 doesn’t have fans. Not too sure they paid close enough to detail. Especially since this is a reused design.

Overall the build quality is excellent! Extremely light and sturdy. There is minimal chassis flex. There are three components of the chassis: lid, base, and input shell. The base is a poly-carbonate with wave design. The lid is magnesium-aluminum and the input shell is magnesium-carbon fiber. Each surface is painted with a fingerprint free eggshell finish.

 Weight is 2.84lbs (1.29kg) and it is extremely well balanced.

Lenovo’s is the largest of the new Googlebook lineup and offers an awesome 15.3 inch OLED screen perfect for running multiple windows or binge watching some shows.

Audio is excellent for a laptop and having the up-firing speakers helps not to muffle the sound. Thankfully it has a headphone port and a host of others that also make this version of the Googlebook standout. Either of the USB-C ports can be used for charging or 10GB/s data transfer. And that still leaves a USB-A 3.2 and an HDMI port.

The keyboard is nice, the keys are a little louder than I would like, not quite a mechanical keyboard decibel, but has the press satisfaction of a solid keyboard. I don’t know if it is the trackpad size, but the palm rejection definitely needs some updating. Since that is the software side, I don’t know if that will come through GoogleOS or or driver support? Specs say it has haptic feedback, but I don’t feel that come through.

As a laptop I love it. But this isn’t just another laptop.

GoogleOS based on AndroidOS, which operates similarly to Android Desktop, with a little ChromeOS still shining through.

GoogleOS feels like a gooey brownie you're trying to cook through but not over do it and you just stuck the toothpick in the for the first time…and its still got some batter on it.

Even though there is a familiarity with the OS coming from Android phones it really helps if you are a Pixel user or at least an Android that doesn’t use its own skin/launcher, there is still a learning curve, as this is not just a straight port of Android or even Android Desktop experience.

Comparing it to ChromeOS, I definitely like the direction Google is going, as this feels like a real OS meant for getting things done. As stated the brownies aren’t done yet, but they will be with some time. Thankfully, though, in this situation, you can have your cake (brownie) and eat it too as out-of-the-box the OS is very usable and useful.

A lot of tech reviewers were riding these hard and understandably so, as the these are priced higher than a Chromebook Plus with the same specs and in some cases higher than a WindowsOS laptop, so the expectations are high and the results didn’t quite match. 

However, I think because there is a lot of familiarity with the OS because of ChromeOS and AndroidOS there were too many assumptions that it is the same or mild iteration with  just a keyboard attached to a massive screen.

But multiple, resizable windows are a massive jump from static windows on comparatively tiny screens.

As a business user, creator, and multiple Chrome Profile aficionado, I don’t know if a Googlebook can be my main laptop yet, but it definitely feels closer than ever.

reviews.title: Not baked enough for release
reviews.content:
I got it early and had to return it.  Too many flaws after a week.  The seamless integration with my Android phone did not exist.  The Google AI promo (12 mos. included) did not work - could not access the perk.  Contacted Google support on that, created a ticket, and still no answer after 2 weeks.  Keystrokes were laggy with the x86 architecture - not sure how they get that to go away.  The settings page was strange - the laptop seemed to think it was a Pixel phone. 

It was all just too much for $1100.

I was really looking forward to the having app open on my phone and then opening on the googebook but I couldn't get that to work every time.  I ended up returning the item since I couldn't find enough features or cool things to justify spending $1100 when I can buy a chromebook for $500 which can do the exact same thing.

reviews.title: Nice Laptop, but with minor issues
reviews.content:
I bought this HP because of the small design, Intel Series 3 CPU/IGPU combo which I thought would give me excellent battery life and gaming performance.
It does, to a point, but not nearly as good as what I had hoped.
The Laptop's gaming performance is not nearly as good with the B390 as the 140V on the games I play, which was surprising.
I was hoping for a significant increase in Frame Rates, along with much better battery life.
I got neither.
The Battery life is mediocre coming from a Series 3 setup.
The reason for that is partially due to HP's smaller battery Whr size, which is about 6 Whr smaller than my ASUS.
For what you pay for and get, you might as well get a Gaming Laptop or get an ASUS that will allow you to play older games.
\The Sound volume is not nearly as loud as I had hoped, because I am hard of hearing, and wanted a LOUD speaker setup, which it was SUPPOSED to be because it has 4 speakers on it.
It is supposed to be loud, but it's not.
My ASUS is far louder than the HP Omnibook Ultra's 4 Speakers, and they sound better too.

reviews.title: Great Laptop in the Rampocalypse Era
reviews.content:
Long time Lenovo user and thought I should give HP a try for this CPU generation. Very happy with this laptop overall. It has a premium feel and look, and it handles both my work and a heavy gaming load without breaking a sweat. I genuinely couldn’t be happier with the performance and build quality from HP.

The biggest drawback is that HP effectively forces you to use their companion software to access performance profiles. If you do a fresh install of Windows 11 and skip HP’s app, the system will aggressively throttle, so having access to HP’s performance profiles is essential to get the performance you paid for.

I also run Fedora 44 on this machine. As of this writing, onboard sound doesn’t work under Fedora yet, and it will likely require a newer kernel before audio support is fully functional. It also would have been much nicer if this laptop shipped with a 2TB SSD by default, given its performance and price bracket.

Interestingly, I also tried the Omnibook X with the Panther Lake X7, and gaming performance on that weaker configuration was actually better than on this X9 model. Overall, I’m still optimistic this laptop will carry me comfortably through Rampocalypse 2026

reviews.title: Perfectly Balanced
reviews.content:
I'll give the short version first. While it's not a powerhouse, the Omnibook 3 offers a beautiful balance of power, battery, and quality.

Let's break it down by section.

Power:
The device itself isn't that powerful, I can't run almost any games and certain programs on this device. The snapdragon processor's main benefit it a quick processing speed with minimal power draw. I use Chrome, a PDF editor and Firefox for my work and home, and none of these applications have issues even running multiple tabs at a single time. This is great for answering email, browsing the web or possible zoom calls.

Battery:
While I'm at work I will usually be using this laptop for around 6 out of the 8 hours in the workday and when I get home I can expect it to be around the 60% mark. The fact that it charges over USB-C makes charging and battery a non issue. I also like to use the OLED screen to watch media when I am off the job and I can say that a 2 hour watch session only drained the battery about 15% which is impressive for the price point.

Quality:
The finish on the laptop is a light, brushed aluminum case which makes it light and fairly durable. The OLED screen helps conserve battery life while also providing vibrant colors and contrast. It comes with 2 USB-C ports, 2 USB-A ports, an HDMI port and an AUX port for headphones as well as a built in camera with privacy slider. I haven't had any issues with overheating either which is great.

The bad:
Sadly there was a misstep on the release of this product with the snapdragon processor that caused crashes about once a day, however there was a bios update for the device that seems to have resolved this issue. There is no expandable ram or storage on this device, which means you get what you pay for. The screen being an OLED is great, however it is a standard display without touchscreen.

Overall this is a great device for work and for media outside of work, would recommend to anyone looking for a work laptop, especially if you can find it on sale.

reviews.title: Great laptop: thin, fast, but battery drains quick
reviews.content:
bought this Dell XPS 13 (Intel Core Ultra 7, 2K, 16GB/512GB) because I loved how sleek and premium it looked - and honestly, it didn’t disappoint. The build quality is top-notch, the graphite finish looks elegant, and it’s incredibly light to carry around. The 2K display is bright, colorful, and perfect for work or streaming. Performance-wise, it’s super snappy. I could run multiple apps, Office, and Chrome tabs without any lag.

However, the only area that let me down a bit was the battery life. During light work, it lasted a solid 5 hours, but when I started running heavier tasks like large spreadsheets, multiple browser windows, or AI tools, the battery drained much faster - sometimes within 2 - 3 hours. The fans also kicked in occasionally under load, which is expected but noticeable.

In the end, I decided to exchange it for another Dell model - still a Dell, but with higher specs and better cooling and battery performance for my workflow. q_a.question: Will it run the cad/cam program Fusion 360 seamlessly?
q_a.answer:
No. 
The specs and features make it great for daily multitasking, office productivity, and web browsing, but NOT modern 3D CAD/CAM software. Fusion 360 relies heavily on the graphics card for viewport performance, 3D modeling, and rendering, while this Dell model uses integrated AMD Radeon Graphics (which also shares system RAM). The high-resolution display means the integrated graphics chip has to work even harder to push pixels: when rotating complex 3D assemblies, you are highly likely to experience stuttering, frame drops, and lag. Note also that the the "U" in 7730U stands for "ultra-low power consumption," so it is optimized to stretch battery life and stay quiet, meaning it will aggressively thermal throttle under the sustained, heavy workloads typical of rendering toolpaths or calculating stress analyses. For basic, minor tasks—like modeling simple 3D geometric shapes, viewing existing files, or handling light 3D printing projects with few parts—the laptop will open and run Fusion 360, but as soon as you work with multi-component assemblies, intricate toolpaths, or cloud/local rendering, the performance will drop significantly. If your goal is seamless, fluid CAD, you should look for a device that features a dedicated graphics card, like the Nvidia RTX 4050 or 4060 and a performance-focused CPU (typically ending in H or HX rather than U).
You really need to do better homework,

reviews.title: Premium Portability at an Affordable Price
reviews.content:
Finding an ultra portable laptop that looks premium and handles everyday productivity at an affordable price has become extremely difficult, but this Dell XPS 13 delivers on nearly every aspect. Right out of the box the “sky” color finish and minimalist aluminum design gives it that premium aesthetic. It is remarkably thin and lightweight, making it effortless to slip into a bag or carry around without feeling weighed down. The edge to edge keyboard layout has virtually no gaps between the keys which gives it a clean, modern look and feels very comfortable once your fingers settle into typing. The built in backlighting makes working in dim lighting or at night completely effortless, and the smooth glass surface along the wrist rest hides the touchpad entirely while remaining very responsive to clicks.

A main draw of this laptop is easily the 13.4 inch 3K touchscreen display. The resolution makes text and spreadsheets look extremely sharp and colors appear vibrant whether you are streaming shows/movies, browsing the web, or editing documents. Having touchscreen functionality built right into a high resolution display makes scrolling through long articles and zooming into details something I`ll always want in a laptop moving forward, and the ultra thin borders around the glass give you maximum screen space in a very compact footprint.

Everyday performance is snappy and reliable thanks to the Intel Core 5 processor paired with fast solid state storage. Programs open quickly, the system boots up in seconds, and moving between multiple browser tabs, streaming audio, and editing documents happens without hesitation or slowdown. Even during continuous use the laptop runs quietly and stays cool enough to keep comfortable on your lap.

Battery efficiency is another big plus for anyone on the move. It easily powers through a typical day of web browsing, emailing, and working on documents without having to track down an outlet. The two high speed USB-C ports keep charging and connecting to external accessories straightforward and keep desktop clutter to a minimum.

Overall, this XPS 13 hits the sweet spot for an everyday premium laptop at an affordable price. It combines an incredible high resolution touchscreen, a lightweight and modern chassis, and dependable day to day performance. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a sleek, efficient, and highly portable computer for work or school.

reviews.title: Tiny and lighweight, perfect for school
reviews.content:
I recently got the Dell XPS 13.4" 3K
touchscreen laptop in the Sky color and so far l've been really happy with it. The unboxing experience felt premium right away. The laptop was packaged nicely and everything was organized well inside the box. As soon as I took it out, the first thing I noticed was how light and sleek it felt. It looks modern without being flashy and the Sky color gives it a clean and elegant look.
Setting it up was surprisingly easy. After turning it on, Windows walked me through the setup process step by step. Connecting to my home WiFi was quick and there were no issues at all. Within a short time I was signed in, updated, and ready to start using it. Even for someone who is not super technical, the setup process is pretty straightforward.

The laptop itself looks fantastic. It is thin, lightweight, and easy to carry around the house. The build quality feels solid and not cheap. The keyboard is comfortable to type on and the large touchpad works smoothly.
The 3K touchscreen is probably my favorite feature. The screen is bright, sharp, and very clear. Videos, websites, and photos all look great on it. The touchscreen is responsive and reacts quickly when tapping or scrolling.

Performance has been good for what I need.
Opening programs, browsing the internet, watching videos, and doing everyday tasks feels smooth. I haven't noticed any annoying lag or freezing. Everything responds quickly enough that I don't have to sit there waiting for things to load. The speakers also sound better than I expected from a laptop this size. The sound is clear and loud enough for videos, online classes, and casual music listening.

One of the main reasons I got this laptop is because I plan to give it to my kid.
Lately she has been borrowing my laptop whenever she needs to do homework or research. Having her own device will make things much easier for both of us. I wanted something that was reliable, easy to use, and light enough for him to carry around. This seems like a good fit. The touchscreen is also nice because it feels more natural for kids who are already used to phones and tablets.

Overall, I'm very satisfied with this purchase. It looks great, feels premium, is easy to set up, and performs well for everyday use. It may not be the most powerful laptop out there, but for web browsing, school work, video streaming, and general day to day use, it does everything I need. My kid is excited to have her own laptop and I think this will serve her well for school and homework for years to come. The only thing I wish is that it came with a few more ports and perhaps a carrying pouch, but that's a small complaint compared to everything else it does well.

reviews.title: An intelligent decision
reviews.content:
I’ve always appreciated the engineering and design that Asus builds into their products.   This is a company that considers how users will use the laptops in daily life.  This laptop is no exception.  It’s an easy recommendation to friends and family knowing that it will not let them down.  When it comes to warranty coverage, they provide support better than most any other company I’ve dealt with.

What I was looking for in a laptop, is the ruggedness and ability to perform typical daily tasks.  Streaming, word processing, spreadsheets, and more.  It’s not a gaming laptop, even though it has a beautiful OLED screen.  I found the battery can last 2+ days.  

Daily use is easy.  The camera supports Windows Hello login.  Bluetooth and WiFi 6E worked flawlessly.  USB A, and USB C ports, as well as HDMI.  

This particular model has a 256GB SSD.  It’s fine for basic local storage needs.  If you store a lot of files locally, the 512GB version may be a better choice.  The SSD is upgradable if your needs change in the future.

I’d strongly recommend this laptop to anyone looking for a versatile, robust, and easy to live with system.

reviews.title: Small, not heavy-for those who need to move around
reviews.content:
This ASUS Zenbook’s pretty lightweight and compact, but it doesn’t feel flimsy at all. The first thing you and anyone else checking it out will spot is the gorgeous OLED screen, perfect for watching any video, especially HDR stuff. You can only get HDR with video streaming.

Getting this computer set up isn’t any harder than other Windows ones. Make sure you’ve got a few hours free to get all the patches and everything else. 

You’ve got 16 GB RAM which is enough for most stuff, but with a Snapdragon chip, a few programs might not run. Like, Adobe Audition just wouldn’t install. Symantec Endpoint Protection 14.5 just wouldn’t install either. Oracle VirtualBox, while it runs, will not run Windows 2000 nor Windows XP in the window. It just doesn’t work with ARM processors.

 This computer isn’t built for fast games since the graphics card shares memory with the motherboard and isn’t a dedicated GPU. Unfortunately, the hard drive’s a solid-state one, but it’s just 256 GB. Loads of the test programs I installed have taken up more than half that space. And to top it off, there’s no slot for an SD or micro SD card, though there are USB ports on the side. But what a shame it is, there’s no memory card slot. Looks like Windows nowadays is pushing everyone to store their data in the cloud. 

The keyboards are not backlighted 

The cool thing about this computer is that it’s not too heavy—sure, it’s heavier than a Microsoft Surface, but it’s still easy enough for a college student to lug to class or a business person to take back and forth to work. It’s quick enough to handle most business apps. I even tested a voice dictation program, and it works in real time perfectly fine. The speakers are awesome for chilling with a Netflix show or whatever streaming you use. 

I had a long YouTube video going, and somehow, without plugging it in, it kept going for about 11 hours before my computer gave out. It’s totally long-lasting for a full school day, and without needing a plug, you can keep going at work as well. 

You’ll find two USB-C connectors on the left, but one’s taken up by the power supply. It’s got an HDMI output, but who even uses those anymore? Plus, there’s also an old-school headphone jack on the left side. You’ll find a regular USB port on the right side. Again, it really is a shame there’s no memory card slot since the hard drive isn’t that large. I know I can use a USB thumb drive or an external hard drive, but since this computer’s made for portability, I don’t really wanna bring anything else with me. 

Is this good for a college kid? I believe so. It’s super easy to take with you since it’s light and pretty small. If you’re looking to play games, it’s not really on the same level as a desktop. Would a business user find this suitable? I think so as well. For the same reason: small, handy to carry, nice screen, really nice to look at all day. Don’t forget to have internet access to back up your data in the cloud. 

Recommended with a slight hesitation, but if you need something small, this should do quite well.

reviews.title: Useful performance with all-day battery life
reviews.content:
ASUS knows a thing or two about laptops - and their Zenbook line is often the sweet spot between price and useful capabilities which is exactly what you find here.  This particular model - the Zenbook 14 with the Snapdragon X1-26-100 - is a rather interesting middle ground in today's market.  Is it right for you?  Read on to find out!

First, let's start with the internals.  You get the Snapdragon X1-26-100 processor (sometimes previously called a Snapdragon X Plus) which is a first generation Snapdragon X chip with 8 cores and 8 threads.  It's an ARM CPU (more on that in a bit) so it gives up a bit of top end performance (and a lot of graphics capability) in exchange for super lower power consumption.  This means less heat is generated (so the laptop runs quieter and cooler) and the battery truly can last all day, or even multiple days in the right circumstances.  Paired with 16GB of memory / RAM and a 256GB SSD, you get a nice a tidy package.  The SSD is an NVMe SSD in size 2280 which can be easily upgraded (taking off the bottom of the laptop is simple with 10 T5 sized screws the bottom pops right off).  The SSD is easily accessible and easily replaced with a new / larger drive at that point.  Internally that's about all that can be replaced / upgraded though the battery is also accessible at that point.

Performance is very snappy in day to day usage with Windows booting up very quickly and typical internet browsing, email, office work, media streaming - there's even power for light media editing / content creation and gaming.  And the battery life (as noted above) is incredible as it really is ALL day.  There's a big caveat there though - because this is an ARM chip, not all software will be compatible though Microsoft and Qualcomm (and others) have been doing a great job and more and more works each day.  Mostly now it will be certain drivers (my Canon printer's custom driver for example doesn't work, but the generic one is fine) or custom software or perhaps the anti-cheat in some games.  On the topic of gaming...this isn't a gaming laptop.  Sure, it can play light games, some emulation and cloud stream games just fine, but don't buy this purposefully for gaming.  It's a great general use laptop that can play some games.

As to the phsyical nature of the laptop, it's a very solid design that looks at home in a professional use case.  The bottom is sort of a steel blue / gray and the top is a bit darker with almost a mottled look to it that is both just a bit different enough to stand out from plain laptops but not SO much different that it looks out of place.  The build quality is the usual solid ASUS build - this thing is built to last.  You get a good selection ports, with the requisite USB-C for charging/data/video (two of these) but also a full-sized / speed USB-A port, an HDMI port and headphone jack, so you're set for connectivity.  The keyboard is backlit and a dream to type on (for a membrane / laptop keyboard at least) with good feel, travel and feedback and the trackpad is nicely sized and easy to use.  The screen is the REAL champ here - a beautiful 2K OLED with deep blacks and great color overall.  It's great for media consumption and day to day usage.

So if you could use a solidly built computer with snappy performance AND all day battery life (and you don't mind the few ARM tradeoffs around compatibility) this could be exactly what you're looking for.  Give it a try today!

reviews.title: Pretty laptop with questionable features
reviews.content:
I always appreciate the Zenbook line of laptops from Asus as a quick and easy reference for friends and family looking for easy to use and enjoy laptops. This one earns an easy recommendation for general use and enjoyment, but there are definitely some nitpicks I have on this particular laptop model. But to keep it short, I will say that the most likely candidates who would enjoy this laptop will be students in non-computer intensive courses of study (e.g., not engineering or computer science) who are just looking to do their online coursework or do some Office or Google productivity writing papers, making presentations, etc. The Snapdragon CPU and RAM combo present here is more than powerful enough and competent for most general users. 

The laptop comes with some features that also help it to be quite competitive in the 2026 ultralight laptop space. You have a traditional USB-A port for helping to plug in legacy products like an older USB-A wireless mouse etc. and a nice HDMI 2.1 port which will make it easy to plug into projectors or monitors without requiring a USB-C adapter as with so many other ultralight notebooks. I wish these USB-C ports could have been Thunderbolt 4 certified for a tad more versatility, especially when this can be found on ultralight competitors several hundred dollars cheaper. User will also enjoy the facial recognition Hello Windows login as well. 

This laptop comes with only 256Gb of storage space with much less than that being available to the user after updates and operating system programs are installed. If you depend on physical storage for files, music, photos, etc., you will want to have caution picking this laptop or have plans for cloud storage or an external hard drive. Gratefully, this laptop is redeemed by having a good amount of RAM that is also quite speedy paired with a very efficient CPU, so I never struggled to multitask on this laptop. Paired with these are quite and efficient fans that, thanks to the excellent Snapdragon ARM CPU, almost never spun up during my normal use cases. The speakers of this laptop are actually quite good for a slim profile laptop! Two bottom firing speakers are present, and they benefit for accuracy from being on a firm surface like a desk or table rather than on your laptop if you want to get the best audio experience out of them. 
Now for some nitpicks. While I love the sharpness, viewing angle, and color accuracy of the OLED screen, it is HIGHLY reflective. When I bring this up, I am talking about sitting in front of a window without direct sunlight and the glare still being so pronounced that the screen has to be tilted just right to see what you are doing. This issue is further compounded by the fact that the screen can only get to 300 nits brightness which is quite dim and is no better than many cheaper IPS panels used on other laptops. And the final couple struggles with this screen is that is not touchscreen and is only 60hz max refresh. I would hope to have this monitor redeem itself beyond just being a pretty OLED screen, but I am not finding it so far. 

Another couple nitpicks regard the trackpad and the keyboard. The trackpad is not fantastic. It does appear to be made of good glass and allows for easy tracking and cursor placement as well as gestures, but the clicks and press of the keyboard are not fantastic. Only the bottom half of the trackpad, maybe even the bottom third is usable for the actual mechanical right and left clicking which is what I prefer. In an era of amazing trackpads, this one just feels like a throwback to 11 years ago when Apple was the only one who knew what they were doing with trackpads.  As a person who has typed on dozens and dozens of unique keyboards in the last 10 years of computer reviews and productivity work, I can tell you that this keyboard struggles with keycaps that feel “slippery”. It is the best explanation I can give. I have a pretty sharp attack and press when I actuate the keys of a keyboard and I have moments where I feel like as I strike downward, my fingers slip to the side or off the intended key I am aiming for entirely. This is causing me to have to throttle down my typing speed a bit compared to what I can normally do on laptops like this. This nitpick aside, the keys, position, and size are great and allow for someone like me who is normal a MacBook user to type very accurately on this keyboard. 

Altogether, for a laptop that is nearly four digits in price, I suppose I would have been happier to have had just a little more going right with this laptop. In this year of 2026, long battery life and AI support are not enough to sell an ultralight laptop. I look for refinement and features across multiple modalities of the laptop, and this one could particularly use a bit more of that. I will mention that I am being pretty harsh and demanding in this review, but truthfully there are no issues here that are truly no-go’s for the laptop. Thanks for reading and I hope you found this review helpful!

reviews.title: My favorite laptop yet
reviews.content: This ASUS Zenbook laptop has exceeded all my expectations! It has a very elegant feel from the moment I unboxed it. There was a beautiful marble blue background with sleek pockets for the cords. The laptop itself is a gorgeous shade of blue that matches the name - it is such a zen shade of blue. While small, it is mighty and feels very sturdy and high quality materials. I am very impressed with the quality all around. The screen truly fills the screen and leaves a very small border around the edge. I also really appreciate that it has an HDMI port - it is so rare to find an  HDMI port in smaller laptops. It uses the usb-c charge port which is all I use in my home. The touch sensitivity of the mousepad is also excellent - it is the smoothest laptop I've used. When watching a video, the color, quality, and refresh rate are great. The speaker quality is something that I find very important and have a hard time being impressed by them; this one has a great balance of settings that don’t require me to connect to headphones or an external speaker. All around, I would recommend this for students or working professionals who need a compact but reliable and high quality item for their role.

reviews.title: High Expectations Met With Ease
reviews.content:
After a good deal of research, I purchased this unit on sale for $999 ($350 discount) August 8, 2026, to replace a 3-year old Zenbook Q420 that was running increasingly hot and noisy. I had mild concerns that 3 customer reviews and 1 professional review noted heat dissipation issues. That has not been my experience. There have been zero instances of heat dissipation issues, and I often comfortably use this unit while it rests in my lap.  Additionally, this unit is almost always completely silent in fan Standard Mode.  The only instances I've ever heard the fans is during application of new BIOS.   

The Snapdragon 18-core, X2 Elite Extreme processor has performed admirably and I'm very pleased with it's performance, particularly the efficiency it provides contributing to a very long battery life.  I'm able to go 2-3 days between charges at 6-10 hours daily use.  It was well worth the $100 upgrade over the much lower performing X Plus option. I've had no day-to-day application compatibility issues with it's ARM architecture.  

The integrated 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM has been sufficient, as has the 60Hz refresh rate since I'm not a gamer. Speakers are adequate.  

The Zabriskie Beige color is quite attractive and looks better than anticipated.  The keyboard is a darker taupe color that contrasts nicely.  The touchpad is disproportionately large in a good way and works well.  Despite it's size, I've experienced no issues with ghost touching.  The Ceraluminum finish does an excellent job of keeping the unit fingerprint free and weight low at a paltry 2.4 lbs.

The 2K OLED display is beautiful and plenty bright at up to 500 nits.  No concerns with 512GB storage - that's far more than I'll ever use.

In summary, this unit has met high expectations and I'm very pleased. Compared to similarly equipped competitors, purchasing this unit from Best Buy at $999 is a great deal.  Highly recommended!

It has the cpu, internal graphics, the OLED screen, high refresh rate, the nits, the touchscreen, the weight, the long battery, the ports, the speed. I had upgraded from an ultra slim laptop that had poor battery life and was struggling to keep up with daily things and it would get hot just from browsing. NOT this one. It's handling all my daily things well with no struggle, and maintains its battery that I don't need to carry the charger with me (for work or cafe lounging). For gaming I've been enjoying Baldurs Gate 3 on it, and I can open up my shopping browser with all the extensions on it with no issue while also running other programs in the background. I have yet to try editing videos or pictures on it, but I'm confident this perform great for it.

The only (minor) critique about it for my case, I would have preferred the USB-C on the left or backside. For the look of it, it looks nice externally (behind the screen), but looking at it normally in front, it tends to look like an everyday office laptop if it wasn't for the beautiful screen. Gives it that sleeper agent laptop feel to it, but it could have done something about it's keys, or added some nice sound/vent grills on it. This is entirely preference of course, but I simply added decals to the keys and will add more to it later to personalize it.

This is also my first ASUS laptop, and I like that they have a feature to have the battery only charge to 80% to protect the battery. There's also features to protect the OLED screen from burn in, so I appreciate that as well. 

Overall, I am really happy with this laptop and have been using it daily. Though I have a dedicated desktop PC that's a powerhouse, it is nice now having a PORTABLE everyday powerhouse for where ever I go.

reviews.title: Powerful, premium, but not perfect
reviews.content:
Product review:
The ROG Zephyrus G16 is one of the best-balanced gaming laptops I’ve used. The OLED display is excellent, the speakers and trackpad are very good, and the overall design feels much more premium and portable than most gaming laptops.

Performance is still very strong and it can handle demanding games at high settings, but there are some compromises. The thin chassis means higher temperatures, noticeable fan noise under load, and the RTX 5080 does not run at the same power level as it does in larger gaming laptops. Battery life is decent for this type of machine, but it still requires some power management if you want to use it away from the charger for several hours.

Overall, I would recommend it to someone who values portability, design, display quality, and strong gaming performance in one device. If your only priority is maximum performance for the money, there are better options, but for a student, traveler, or creator who needs one powerful laptop for everything, the G16 makes a lot of sense.

q_a.question: Why does this laptop feels like a vivobook?
q_a.answer: This UM3405GA ( Zenbook 14 OLED) laptop shares design traits with the Vivobook line, both use similar 14-inch 16:10 aspect ratio screens. The differences are, the Zenbook uses uses premium aluminum-alloy, while Vivobooks frequently mix aluminum lids with plastic bottom covers. The Zenbook chassis  is physically thinner and weighs less, whereas Vivobooks are typically heavier. Additonally, Zenbook, like this UM3405GA laptop, features dual USB4/Thunderbolt 4 ports, whereas a Vivobook will typically feature slower USB 3.2 ports.

reviews.title: A SUPER ASUS TUF Gaming A16 16" Laptop!
reviews.content:
I received the ASUS TUF Gaming A16 16"  Gaming Laptop and have been extremely happy with the speed of this laptop!  But before I get into that ....

It's always amazing to me the improvements that the Manufacturers make every year to  the packaging and setup of computer products each year.   This ASUS gaming laptop is no exception.   Packaging was sturdy and well insulated.  Everything had a "place" in the box!  The very limited "documentation" was interesting, but as it turns out, you really don't need it.

Turning on the laptop and starting the setup process was simple and easy.  It seemed like the amount of "updates" this laptop needed at setup was extremely limited, so ASUS did a great job making sure it was "current" before shipping it out to customers.

I really like the speed of this laptop.   Normally, when you have a few windows open with apps, past systems would have a tendency to "slow down" .. Not this baby!    One thing I really like - because I'm a keyboard person - is that since a 16" screen, the laptop had a separate numeric pad.   I do a lot of "number crunching" so I find all the 14" and 15" laptops  are harder for me to be efficient when using Excel.   This ASUS has a much-welcomed keyboard layout.

Even though it's a 16" laptop, it's not heavy like the older 16s" were.   I'm looking forward to using it a lot, especially since we travel frequently and I always need to have a laptop handy.

Accessing my wireless internet was a breeze and I was able to easily access my remote wireless printer with no hiccups.   The USB-C connectors were good, but I always need "one more" for things I connect to my laptop, even while traveling.

IT'S A FANTASTIC LAPTOP THAT I WOULD RECOMMEND TO ANYONE....
